lead: Today our Church honours the four Evangelists together: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. The Epistle traces the chain by which faith reaches anyone at all: someone is sent, someone proclaims, someone hears, someone believes and calls on the Lord. “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” The Gospel is the last page of Matthew, where the risen Lord sends the eleven to all nations and promises, “I am with you always.” The four Evangelists stand in that sending: what the apostles preached, they wrote down for every generation. The key words are sent, hear and with you.

r.h: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, around AD 57, to a church he had not yet visited. Chapters 9–11 wrestle with a question that grieved him deeply: why had most of his own people, Israel, not accepted Jesus as the Messiah? He begins with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” (9:2). He ends by saying that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26) and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).

Just before today's verses Paul has quoted the prophet Joel: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (10:13). Now he traces, link by link, the chain that makes such calling possible.
str: vv. 14–15: the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent; Isaiah 52:7.
vv. 16–17: not all have obeyed; faith comes from what is heard (Isaiah 53:1).
v. 18: the message has gone out to all the earth (Psalm 19:4).
vv. 19–20: Moses and Isaiah: God found by those who did not seek him (Deuteronomy 32:21; Isaiah 65:1).

¶ The next verse (10:21) shows God holding out his hands “all day long” to his people. The passage ends not in rejection but in God's patience, and chapter 11 opens: “has God rejected his people? By no means!”
kw: From this verb comes the word apostle. Preaching in the Church is not self-appointed: “how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent?” The Evangelists wrote within this sending, and their books carry the preaching of the apostles.
The verb of Isaiah 52:7 in the Greek Old Testament, used of the messenger running over the mountains to Jerusalem to say, “Your God reigns.” Our word Evangelist comes from the same root.

The same word means both the act of hearing and the message that is heard. Faith begins as an answer to a word that comes to us from outside. Paul adds “through the word of Christ”: the message is about Christ, and in it Christ himself speaks.
vv: And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
In Isaiah the feet belong to a runner bringing news of peace to Jerusalem after the exile. They are beautiful not for their shape but for the news they carry, and for the long road they have walked.
So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
Faith is personal, but it is never private in its origin. No one gives it to himself. It comes through a voice: a parent, a catechist, a priest, a book of the Gospels read aloud.
Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

Psalm 19 says this of the heavens, which declare God's glory without speech. Paul applies it to the apostles' preaching. He quotes the Greek Old Testament, “their voice”; the Hebrew text has “their line”.
I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.
From Isaiah 65:1. Paul reads it of the Gentiles who came to faith without having looked for it. God goes ahead of every search.
ch: The Church reads this passage as the charter of her preaching. The Catechism quotes verses 14–15 to show that no one can give himself the mandate to preach the Gospel: the minister of Christ is sent and speaks with an authority he has received (CCC 875). The Second Vatican Council teaches that among all the Scriptures the Gospels have a special place, because they are the principal witness to the life and teaching of the incarnate Word, and that the Church has always held that the four Gospels are of apostolic origin (Dei Verbum 18). Paul's sorrow for his own people is also the Church's: God has not rejected Israel, and the Church relates to the Jewish people as to those to whom God first spoke (CCC 839).

r.h: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations
set: These are the last verses of Matthew's Gospel. On Easter morning the risen Lord met the women and gave them a message for “my brothers”: go to Galilee, and there they will see me (28:10). Galilee is where Jesus began his preaching, “Galilee of the Gentiles” (4:15). Matthew does not describe the Ascension. His Gospel ends with a promise of presence.
Matthew's Gospel began with the name Emmanuel, “God is with us” (1:23). It ends with “I am with you always”. The whole book lies between these two sayings.
str: v. 16: the eleven go to the mountain in Galilee.
v. 18: all authority given to Jesus.
vv. 19–20a: go, make disciples, baptize, teach.
v. 20b: I am with you always.
kw: The one main command in the sentence; going, baptizing and teaching serve it. A disciple is a learner who follows the master and lives with him. The mission is not only to win agreement but to form lives.

During his ministry Jesus sent the Twelve first to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6). Now the circle opens to every people. Israel is not left out. The promise to Abraham, that in him “all the families of the earth shall be blessed”, is reaching its goal (Genesis 12:3).
Baptism is “in the name”, singular, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The Greek suggests being plunged into, and belonging to, the one God who is three persons.
vv: When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.

Matthew is honest. On the mountain of the risen Lord, worship and hesitation stand side by side. The verb for doubt is the one Jesus used to Peter sinking in the waves: “why did you doubt?” (14:31). Jesus does not send the hesitant away. In the next verse he comes near to them.
All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

Daniel saw one like a son of man, to whom was given dominion over all peoples (Daniel 7:13–14). The risen Jesus speaks as that Son of Man. The mission rests on his authority, not on the strength of the eleven.
Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
The clearest naming of the Trinity in the Gospels. The early Church baptized with these words; the Didache, a very early Christian handbook, already gives them.
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
Not “I will be” but “I am”. Many readers hear in it an echo of God's name revealed to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). The Church goes out with the Lord already at her side.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses as the origin of the Church's missionary mandate (CCC 849), and teaches that we are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, not in their names, for there is only one God (CCC 233). St Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around AD 180, held that there can be neither more nor fewer than four Gospels, as there are four winds and four quarters of the world, and he linked them with the four living creatures around God's throne (Against Heresies 3.11.8, in substance; Revelation 4:6–7). St Jerome later gave the symbols that Christian art still uses: the man for Matthew, the lion for Mark, the ox for Luke and the eagle for John.

qa: Why four Gospels and not one?

The early Church received four written witnesses to the one Gospel of Jesus Christ, each rooted in the apostles' preaching. Their differences in order and detail are like four witnesses describing the same events. In the second century Tatian wove them into a single account, the Diatessaron, which was read in Syriac-speaking churches for a long time; Mar Aprem wrote a commentary on it. In the end the Church kept the four, because each brings out something of the one Lord in its own way (Dei Verbum 18–19; CCC 125–127).

Matthew and John are counted by the Church's tradition among the Twelve. Early writers link Mark with Peter and Luke with Paul. Many scholars today think the Gospels as we have them were written down between about AD 65 and 100, drawing on the preaching and tradition of the apostles. The Church holds them to be of apostolic origin and to hand on faithfully what Jesus really did and taught (Dei Verbum 18–19).
rite: Our Church honours the four Evangelists on one day. In the Holy Qurbono the reading of the Gospel is surrounded with signs of honour: lighted candles, incense, and the people standing to listen. The Gospel is announced with the name of the apostle or evangelist who wrote it, and the people answer with praise to the Lord who sent him. The Syriac Churches once read the four Gospels woven into one, in the Diatessaron, and then returned to the four separate books. Today we thank God for the four voices through which the one Gospel has reached Kerala and our own homes.
study: Paul says that faith comes from what is heard. Through whose voice did I first hear the Gospel, and have I thanked God for that person?
Matthew is honest that “some doubted”. What doubt do I bring to the Lord, and what does it mean to me that he still comes near?
Which Gospel do I know best, and which least? How could our family read one Gospel through, slowly, in the coming months?
